title: What "No Editorial Spin" Means in Practice

sources.label: scripts/prompts.js — the drafting prompts and their quality rules
docs/BOTH-SIDES.md — the both-sides eligibility, attribution and order rules
scripts/fetch_bill_cr.js — the Congressional Record quote extractor
docs/QA-LOOP.md — the claim-level fidelity and coverage/omission passes

claims.claim: The site does not evaluate whether a bill is good policy.
The site does not use framing that implies a political conclusion.
claims.sourceSpan: RULE 7 — NO EDITORIAL ADJECTIVES OR FRAMING IN ZONE 1 OR ZONE 2

claims.claim: The site does not suppress information because of its political valence: a coverage pass flags any material provision the analysis leaves out.
The site does not amplify one side either: manufacturing an opposing side is treated as a neutrality violation equal to taking one.
claims.sourceSpan: **False balance is a neutrality violation equal to picking a winner.**

claims.claim: Analyses describe the specific statutory text a bill adds, modifies, or removes.
claims.sourceSpan: added = new programs or rights created by this bill

claims.claim: How members voted is recorded from the official roll call.
Floor statements are attributed to the member by name and reproduced from the Congressional Record.
claims.sourceSpan: // Every sentence of the quote must appear verbatim in the CR

claims.claim: The site does not characterize intent; it reports the stated position.
claims.sourceSpan: **Never characterize motive.** Report the stated position.

claims.claim: The site prefers the statute’s own terms over a coalition’s preferred framing, using "estate tax" rather than "death tax" and "fetus" rather than "unborn child".
Words that characterize intent, significance, prominence or political valence are prohibited in the analysis fields.
claims.sourceSpan: Do not use words that characterize intent, significance, prominence, or political valence.

claims.claim: The site does not evaluate which side of an argument is correct — it describes rather than evaluates.
Every argument in a both-sides section is attributed to a named holder and backed by a retrieved document.
claims.sourceSpan: Every argumentative claim names its holder

claims.claim: The acceptable backing documents are the organization’s own statement or letter, a recorded vote, a Statement of Administration Policy, or a member’s own words.

A both-sides section appears only when opposition is on the record through a near-party-line or closely split recorded vote, a formal opposition letter or statement from a named organization, a Statement of Administration Policy or veto threat, or on-record statements against from named members.
claims.sourceSpan: A both-sides section appears ONLY when opposition is **on the record** through at least one of:

claims.claim: A bill that passed by voice vote, unanimous consent, or a lopsided tally gets no opposition section, and the structural fact is stated instead.
claims.sourceSpan: A voice vote, a lopsided tally, or unanimous consent means the both-sides frame does not apply.

claims.claim: Inventing a second side is treated as the same failure as taking a side.
claims.sourceSpan: Inventing a second side to look even is the same failure, in the other direction, as taking a side.

claims.claim: The site does not suppress detail that cuts against a bill’s stated purpose: a coverage pass lists the source’s most material provisions and flags any that the analysis omits.
claims.sourceSpan: list the bill's most material provisions; any absent or misleadingly buried = an OMISSION flag

claims.claim: Significance is conveyed through structural facts rather than adjectives.
claims.sourceSpan: Significance comes from **structural facts** — sponsorship, stage, vote margins,

claims.claim: The same descriptive standard is applied regardless of which coalition a bill comes from — the editorial-label ban is stated as an absolute, not per-party.
